# Core Features: Skill Gateway

Published URL: https://jarvisregistry.com/features/skill-gateway/
Source Markdown: docs/features/skill-gateway.md

# Skill Gateway

The **Skill Gateway** is a private, organization-managed catalog for authoring, importing, governing, and distributing approved AI skills. Skills remain private by default and are shared through Registry ACLs; the [AI Skills CLI](ai-skills-cli.md) delivers accessible skills to supported developer tools without publishing private content to a public marketplace.

## Manage Skills in the Registry

Skills can be created and edited through the Registry UI or API. Teams can organize them with categories and tags, track a version, and enable or disable a skill as its availability changes. Each skill can include its `SKILL.md` content and supporting text or binary files.

Supporting files are validated before they are stored. Paths must be normalized relative POSIX paths, individual files are limited to 5 MiB, a skill can contain up to 200 files, and the total supporting-file payload is limited to 10 MiB. These limits keep skill content predictable for both the Registry and downstream sync clients.

## Govern Access with ACLs

Skills are private resources by default. The Registry applies resource-level ACL permissions so access can be scoped to the authenticated user and the individual skill:

| Permission | What it allows |
| --- | --- |
| **VIEW** | List, inspect, and download an accessible skill and its files |
| **EDIT** | Change skill metadata, content, and supporting files |
| **DELETE** | Remove the skill or its supporting files |
| **SHARE** | Manage access for other users or groups |

The skill creator receives full permissions, while other users receive only the access explicitly granted to them. Listing and content endpoints filter by ACL, so an inaccessible skill is not presented as an available delivery target.

<span id="import-from-github"></span>

## Import from Git Providers

Skill Gateway supports any Git provider, including GitHub and GitLab. Repository import moves skills in one direction: source repository to Registry. The Registry does not push changes back to the source repository.

The [GitHub source sync API](../design/skill-sync-source-api.md) documents the GitHub App connection and provider-specific fields used in the [private skill walkthrough](../walkthroughs/private-skill-lifecycle.md). These examples describe the GitHub integration rather than limiting Skill Gateway to one provider.

The documented GitHub import pipeline resolves the selected ref to a commit, downloads an immutable repository snapshot, and discovers skill folders containing `SKILL.md` in configured repository paths. It safely extracts those paths with protections for traversal, links, oversized files, and decompression bombs. Each discovered skill is parsed and validated before the sync applies the batch atomically; item-level errors are retained so operators can see which skills were skipped or failed without losing the job's overall report.

## Private Hosting and Governance

The enterprise benefit is controlled distribution:

- Keep organization-approved skills in a private Registry deployment.
- Scope access per user, group, and skill resource through ACLs.
- Protect source-provider and Registry credentials behind the configured authentication flow.
- Share approved content with developers without publishing private skills to a public marketplace.

## Deliver Skills to Developer Tools

Skill Gateway supports skill consumers including Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor. The [AI Skills CLI](ai-skills-cli.md) delivers accessible Registry skills into personal or project environments using its documented directory modes. Use the client-specific setup for skill loading; the CLI repository contains the operational installation and command reference. MCP client connections are a separate capability.

## Common Questions

### What is a private skill marketplace?

A private skill marketplace is an organization-controlled catalog for approved skills, with access limited by the organization's policies. Jarvis Skill Gateway provides Registry-based authoring, Git-provider import, version and metadata management, and ACL-governed sharing rather than publishing private skills to a public marketplace.

### Which developer tools can receive Registry skills?

Supported consumers include Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor. See [AI Skills CLI](ai-skills-cli.md) for the documented CLI modes and delivery workflow, and verify loading in the selected client. Skill delivery is distinct from connecting an MCP-compatible client to the gateway.

## Next Steps

- [AI Skills CLI](ai-skills-cli.md) - distribute Registry skills to local developer tools
- [RBAC & Scopes](../design/scopes.md) - understand identity scopes and access control
- [Security Control Design](../design/security-design.md) - see how authentication and ACLs compose
- [GitHub source sync API](../design/skill-sync-source-api.md) - configure repository import and inspect sync jobs
- [Private skill lifecycle walkthrough](../walkthroughs/private-skill-lifecycle.md) - verify import, updates, and access removal

# Core Features: AI Skills CLI

Published URL: https://jarvisregistry.com/features/ai-skills-cli/
Source Markdown: docs/features/ai-skills-cli.md

# AI Skills CLI

The **Jarvis Registry CLI** delivers accessible private Registry skills into local developer environments. It lets developers consume organization-approved skills without manually copying content or handling Registry credentials in scripts. Skill Gateway supports consumers including Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Cursor; this page describes the CLI's documented directory modes.

The [Skill Gateway](skill-gateway.md) is where skills are authored, imported, governed, and shared. The CLI is where an authenticated developer reconciles the skills they can access into a local integration.

For installation, platform requirements, configuration, command reference, and troubleshooting, see the [Jarvis Registry CLI repository](https://github.com/ascending-llc/jarvis-registry-cli).

## Shared Workflow

Configure the Registry and sign in:

```sh
jarvis-registry configure
jarvis-registry auth login
```

Choose the sync mode for your client. The command syntax is:

```text
jarvis-registry skills sync --mode <claude|codex|copilot>
```

Replace the placeholder with one mode. For example, to sync for Claude Code:

```sh
jarvis-registry skills sync --mode claude
```

Use `--mode codex` for Codex or `--mode copilot` for GitHub Copilot. These mode names select local directory conventions; they are not an exhaustive list of Skill Gateway consumers.

The CLI authenticates against the Registry and syncs only the skills available to the signed-in user. Browser sign-in normally stores credentials in the operating system keyring. On Linux without a usable keyring, it falls back to a plaintext `~/.jarvis-registry/credentials.json` file with mode `0600` and a first-use warning. The explicit `local.credentials.file_only: true` option also uses that file; it is not encrypted. Review the [credential-storage options](https://github.com/ascending-llc/jarvis-registry-cli/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md) for the machine running the CLI.

## Consumers and CLI Modes

| Consumer | Documented CLI mode |
| --- | --- |
| [Claude Code](https://docs.anthropic.com/en/docs/claude-code/skills) | `claude` |
| [Codex](https://developers.openai.com/codex/skills/) | `codex` |
| [GitHub Copilot](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/concepts/agents/about-agent-skills) | `copilot` |

Cursor is also a supported Skill Gateway consumer. Its [Agent Skills guide](https://cursor.com/docs/skills) includes project `.agents/skills/`, the project destination written by `codex` mode. Verify skill loading in your Cursor version. The CLI command reference documents the three modes above; it does not define a separate `cursor` mode.

For these CLI modes, skills can be synchronized for personal use across projects or for a specific project. The CLI handles the local layout and invocation conventions for each mode.

## Claude Code MCP Connection

Claude-mode sync also writes the Registry MCP connection into the generated plugin's `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`. Run `jarvis-registry skills sync --mode claude` for the personal plugin at `~/.claude/skills/jarvis-registry/`, or add a project path for `<path>/.claude/skills/jarvis-registry/`. Configure `registry.base_url` as the deployment origin; the CLI appends `/gateway/proxy/mcpgw/mcp` and includes no credentials in the manifest.

Automatic loading of plugins from skills directories requires Claude Code v2.1.157 or later; see the [Claude Code release notes](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md#21157). After the first sync or a connection change, reload the plugin or start a new Claude Code session. For a project plugin, start Claude Code from that project directory and complete any workspace trust and MCP approval. Open `/mcp`, select the plugin's Registry connection, and complete MCP OAuth if prompted. This authorization is separate from the CLI's skills login. Confirm that the plugin's discovery tools are listed and that a read-only discovery call succeeds; there is no need to add a separate manual MCP definition.

Existing manually configured connections remain untouched. If a duplicate appears, temporarily isolate it while checking the plugin connection and use the tool names actually displayed by Claude Code. See the [CLI getting started guide](https://github.com/ascending-llc/jarvis-registry-cli/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md#claude-code) for personal/project loading, plugin precedence, authentication, and sync verification steps.

Codex and Copilot modes continue to deliver skills; they do not install MCP plugins through this sync flow.

## Governed Delivery

Sync is access-aware and repeatable: after a successful sync, the CLI delivers newly accessible skills, updates changed content, and removes managed local skills the user can no longer access. Revoking Registry access does not instantly recall files already copied to a developer's machine, and the CLI cannot remove independent copies outside its managed paths.

Local cleanup depends on the integration and scope. Personal-scoped Codex and Copilot sync leave skill-name collisions untouched by default; choosing an interactive replacement or override can remove the conflicting directory's contents. Those replacement options do not apply to Claude or project scope. Project-scoped Codex and Copilot sync treat their managed directories as CLI-owned and remove entries not in the current managed set. Review the [CLI getting started guide](https://github.com/ascending-llc/jarvis-registry-cli/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md) before scheduling sync or using replacement options.

## Learn More

- [Jarvis Registry CLI repository](https://github.com/ascending-llc/jarvis-registry-cli) - product source and full documentation
- [CLI setup guide](https://github.com/ascending-llc/jarvis-registry-cli/blob/main/docs/setup.md) - installation and configuration
- [CLI getting started guide](https://github.com/ascending-llc/jarvis-registry-cli/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md) - integration workflow and sync behavior

## Next Steps

- [Skill Gateway](skill-gateway.md) - author, import, govern, and share the skills delivered by the CLI
- [Private skill lifecycle walkthrough](../walkthroughs/private-skill-lifecycle.md) - verify import, updates, and access removal

# Core Features: AWS AgentCore Federation

Published URL: https://jarvisregistry.com/features/agentcore-federation/
Source Markdown: docs/features/agentcore-federation.md

# AgentCore Federation
AgentCore Federation connects an external Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateway to Jarvis Registry so platform admins can import and govern resources from one control plane.

<div style="text-align: center; margin: 1.5rem 0; position: relative; display: inline-block;">
	<a href="https://ascendingdc.com/jarvis-ai/videos/aws-agentcore-federation-with-jarvis-registry-access-governed-agents-from-any-interface/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" style="display: inline-block; position: relative;">
		<img src="https://img.youtube.com/vi/JTziFEg1vg0/maxresdefault.jpg" alt="AgentCore Federation — watch demo" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; display:block; border-radius:8px;" />
		<span style="position:absolute; left:50%; top:50%; transform:translate(-50%,-50%); background:rgba(0,0,0,0.5); width:84px; height:84px; border-radius:50%; display:flex; align-items:center; justify-content:center;">
			<svg width="40" height="40" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true">
				<path d="M8 5v14l11-7L8 5z" fill="#fff" />
			</svg>
		</span>
	</a>
</div>

This page focuses on the operational flow:

1. Admin creates a federation connection in the UI.
2. Registry syncs MCP servers and A2A agents from AgentCore.
3. Admin reviews imported resources and shares them using the same ACL model used across the registry.

---

## Federation Creation Flow

A federation starts with a simple creation form in Jarvis Registry.

Admins provide:

- **Federation Name** — friendly name for the AgentCore source
- **Connection Settings** — aws region and agentcore assume role
- **Resource Tags Filter** — sync only specific tagged resources or sync all.

![AgentCore Federation Create Form](../img/agentcore-federation.png)

After save, Jarvis Registry validates the connection and establishes the federation link.

---

## Automatic Import from AgentCore

Once federation is active, Jarvis Registry can automatically pull resources from AgentCore.

Imported resources include:

- **MCP servers** exposed by the federated AgentCore gateway
- **A2A agents** available from the same federated source

The sync process normalizes external metadata into registry-native entries so they appear in the same catalog experience as local resources.

---

## Admin Governance After Sync

Federated resources are not automatically open to all users. Admins still control visibility and access.

After sync, admins can:

- Keep imported resources private for validation
- Share with specific users or groups
- Publish to everyone with VIEW access when ready

The sharing model is exactly the same as other resources in Jarvis Registry:

- MCP resources follow the same controls as [MCP Server Registry share panel](mcp-gateway-registry.md#sharing-a-server)
- Agent resources follow the same controls as [A2A Agent Registry share panel](a2a-gateway-registry.md#sharing-an-agent)

Security enforcement (authentication, RBAC, ACL) remains consistent for federated and local resources. See [Security Control Design](../design/security-design.md).

- [Workflow Orchestration](workflow-orchestration.md) — How AgentCore agents participate in multi-agent, MCP, and skill workflows
- [MCP Server Registry](mcp-gateway-registry.md) — Sharing and lifecycle for MCP resources
- [A2A Agent Registry](a2a-gateway-registry.md) — Sharing and lifecycle for agent resources
- [Registry Endpoint](registry-endpoint.md) — How clients discover and invoke federated resources
- [AgentCore Federation API](../design/federation-api.md) — Configuration and synchronization API reference
- [Federation Guide](../design/federation.md) — Registry-to-registry federation architecture

**Product page & demo**

- Federation demo and product notes on ASCENDING: [AgentCore & AI Foundry federation](https://ascendingdc.com/jarvis-ai/agent-gateway/agentcore-aifoundry-federation/).

This page focuses on the operational flow:

1. Admin creates a federation connection in the UI.
2. Registry syncs A2A agents from the Azure AI Foundry workspace.

---

## Federation Creation Flow

A federation starts with a simple creation form in Jarvis Registry.

Admins provide:

- **Federation Name** — friendly name for the Azure AI Foundry source
- **Connection Settings** — Azure subscription ID, resource group, AI Foundry workspace name, and Entra ID tenant ID
- **Resource Tags Filter** — sync only specific tagged agents or sync all

After save, Jarvis Registry validates the connection using the provided Entra ID credentials and establishes the federation link.

---

## Automatic Import from Azure AI Foundry

Once federation is active, Jarvis Registry automatically pulls agents from the connected workspace.

Imported resources include:

- **A2A agents** available from the Azure AI Foundry Agent Service

Azure AI Foundry agents use non-standard AgentCard discovery paths (e.g. `agentCard/v0.3` rather than `/.well-known/agent-card.json`) and require Entra ID RBAC role assignments before invocation. The sync process normalizes these platform-specific differences — storing the custom discovery paths and auth prerequisites — so imported agents appear in the same catalog experience as local resources and can be invoked without platform-specific client code.

---

## Admin Governance After Sync

Federated agents are not automatically open to all users. Admins still control visibility and access.

After sync, admins can:

- Keep imported agents private for validation
- Share with specific users or groups
- Publish to everyone with VIEW access when ready

The sharing model is exactly the same as other resources in Jarvis Registry:

- Agent resources follow the same controls as [A2A Agent Registry share panel](a2a-gateway-registry.md#sharing-an-agent)

Security enforcement (authentication, RBAC, ACL) remains consistent for federated and local resources. See [Security Control Design](../design/security-design.md).

# Core Features: Workflow Orchestration

Published URL: https://jarvisregistry.com/features/workflow-orchestration/
Source Markdown: docs/features/workflow-orchestration.md

# Workflow Orchestration

Jarvis Registry workflow orchestration lets you compose A2A agents, MCP tools, and skills into multi-step pipelines that complete complex tasks — with conditional logic, parallel execution, and human approval gates.

<div style="text-align: center; margin: 1.5rem 0;">
  <iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/vQkYLIabrZg?si=pleyYr-B4XZtg6_0" title="Workflow orchestration with Jarvis Registry" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>
</div>

---

## Composing Agents, Skills, and MCP Tools

A workflow step can invoke any resource registered in Jarvis Registry:

- **A2A Agent step** — delegate a subtask to a worker agent (AgentCore, Azure AI Foundry, or self-hosted) and forward its output to the next step.
- **MCP Tool step** — invoke a specific tool, prompt, or resource from any registered MCP server and pass the response onward.
- **Skill step** — describe the capability needed in natural language; the Skill Gateway resolves the best-matched agent or MCP server at runtime.

Steps are chained by passing outputs forward. The gateway handles transport negotiation, auth prerequisites, and ACL enforcement at each hop.

---

## Workflow Logic

### Sequential steps

Sequential execution is the default: each step runs after the previous one completes and its output becomes available to the next step.

### Parallel execution

Steps that don't depend on each other can run concurrently. The workflow waits for all parallel branches to complete before merging results into the next step.

```
Step 1 (fetch data)
  ├── Step 2a (analyze sentiment)   ─┐
  └── Step 2b (extract entities)    ─┤ parallel
                                     ↓
                              Step 3 (summarize)
```

### Conditional branching

Route execution to different steps based on earlier outputs — for example, escalate to a senior agent if a confidence score falls below a threshold, or skip a step when cached data is available.

### Approval gates

Pause a workflow and require explicit human or system approval before proceeding. A gate may be configured with timeouts and escalation targets (approve, reject, auto-escalate).

### Retry and fallback

Configure retry limits, backoff, and fallback targets so workflows can recover from transient failures without failing the entire pipeline.

---

## Step configuration (common options)

- **Timeouts** — per-step execution timeout.
- **Retries** — retry policy (count, backoff, jitter).
- **Parallelism** — max concurrency for parallel branches.
- **Approval policy** — approvers, timeout, and escalation.
- **Fallbacks** — alternate targets or compensating actions on failure.

---

## Demo & external resources

- Product/demo pages on Ascending DC:
  - [A2A Agent Registry](https://ascendingdc.com/jarvis-ai/agent-registry/) — product demo and docs for agent registry and cataloging.
  - [Agent Gateway](https://ascendingdc.com/jarvis-ai/agent-gateway/) — overview of the agent gateway product and demo pages.
  - [MCP Gateway](https://ascendingdc.com/jarvis-ai/mcp-gateway/) — product page for the MCP gateway and integration examples.

# Core Features: Registry Endpoint

Published URL: https://jarvisregistry.com/features/registry-endpoint/
Source Markdown: docs/features/registry-endpoint.md

# Registry Endpoint

The Registry Endpoint is the single MCP entry point that AI copilots use to access your enterprise tools and agents.

Instead of configuring every MCP server or A2A agent one by one, you connect your client once to Jarvis Registry. From there, discovery, authorization, token handling, and proxy routing are managed centrally.

---

## One Endpoint for Multiple Copilots

Jarvis Registry supports common MCP clients and coding assistants through the same endpoint model:

- VS Code
- Cursor
- Claude Desktop
- ChatGPT
- Microsoft Copilot
- AWS Kiro
- AWS QuickSuite

All of them connect to the same registry endpoint pattern and then receive only the resources the user is allowed to access.

![Endpoint Configuration](../img/endpoint-instruction.png)

### Copy the configuration generated for your deployment

Use the Registry's client configuration dialog to generate the endpoint URL and configuration for your client. It includes the deployment's configured base path; do not add `/gateway` unless that is your deployment's base path.

For example, a VS Code `.vscode/mcp.json` configuration for a Registry hosted at `https://registry.example.com` **with `BASE_PATH=/gateway`** is:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "jarvis-registry": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://registry.example.com/gateway/proxy/mcpgw/mcp"
    }
  }
}
```

A root-mounted deployment instead uses `https://registry.example.com/proxy/mcpgw/mcp`. The example hostname is a placeholder. Other clients use their own configuration format, so copy their generated configuration rather than reusing the VS Code JSON unchanged.

![Claude example screenshot](../img/endpoint-claude-example.png)

---

## Automatic IdP Authentication

Client access is automatically integrated with your enterprise IdP through the registry auth layer.

What this means in practice:

1. User signs in through the configured IdP flow.
2. Registry validates tokens and resolves user groups/scopes.
3. All downstream MCP/agent access decisions are based on the authenticated user identity.

This gives users SSO-style access and gives admins centralized identity control without per-tool credential setup in each copilot.

Registry sign-in does not replace authorization to a downstream business service. If a registered server requires its own OAuth identity, the user may also need to complete that service's authorization flow. Gateway access and backend record permissions remain separate checks.

For identity setup details, see [IDP Integration](auth-server.md).

---

## Service Discovery with RBAC + ACL Context

The endpoint supports intelligent discovery so clients can find the right capability with natural language context.

Discovery is permission-aware by default:

- **RBAC filter**: endpoint-level permissions based on user role/scope
- **ACL filter**: resource-level permissions for specific MCP servers and agents
- **Context matching**: discovery ranks tools by relevance to the current task

Clients use `discover_servers` to find MCP servers and `discover_agents` to find agents. These public tools return resources the caller is authorized to access. The gateway's `execute_tool` tool invokes a selected MCP tool through the Registry; successful discovery does not bypass the invocation checks.

This prevents accidental exposure while still enabling fast, context-aware tool selection.

![VSCode example screenshot](../img/endpoint-vscode-example.png)

---

## OAuth Elicitation Support

Some downstream tools require OAuth re-authentication during use. The Registry Endpoint supports elicitation-style user prompts so clients can recover without manual backend troubleshooting.

When needed, the flow is:

1. A tool call detects missing/expired downstream OAuth authorization.
2. Registry triggers an elicitation/auth prompt back to the client.
3. User completes authentication.
4. Registry resumes the tool path with refreshed authorization.

This keeps the interaction in-session and reduces failed tool calls caused by token expiry.

---

## Agent Path Routing Through Registry Proxy

Users can also call agents directly by their defined path through the registry proxy.

That enables:

- Consistent routing for both MCP servers and A2A agents
- Policy enforcement at the gateway layer
- Easier debugging and targeted testing of a specific agent endpoint

Direct routes still check the applicable server or agent resource permissions. Review the telemetry configured for that route rather than assuming it emits every field needed for an investigation.

The MCP direct-connect proxy does **not** enforce the Registry's server-wide `disabledTools` list. That list hides disabled tools from `discover_servers` and rejects them through `execute_tool`; it is not a per-user tool permission. See [MCP Tool Enablement API](../design/mcp-tool-enablement-api.md) before treating gateway and direct-proxy routes as equivalent.

---

## How the Endpoint Fits the Platform

The Registry Endpoint is the runtime layer that connects all feature areas:

- Resources come from [MCP Server Registry](mcp-gateway-registry.md), [A2A Agent Registry](a2a-gateway-registry.md), and federated sources.
- Security comes from IdP auth, RBAC scopes, and ACL checks.
- Discovery and invocation happen through one consistent interface for every supported copilot.

# Core Features: Observability

Published URL: https://jarvisregistry.com/features/observability/
Source Markdown: docs/features/observability.md

# Observability

Jarvis instruments every layer of the platform with OpenTelemetry and ships that telemetry through a vendor-neutral pipeline. The goal is simple: **connect to whatever observability backend you already use** — Grafana, New Relic, Datadog, Splunk, Grafana Cloud, Honeycomb, and others — without changing a line of application code.

Two complementary signals tell the whole story: **platform metrics** — what the registry, gateway, and auth server are doing — and **agent traces** — what the LLMs behind the gateway are doing. Both are emitted as OTLP and both flow through a shared OpenTelemetry collector, which is where you choose your backend.

---

## Pipeline at a Glance

Platform components export **metrics**; agents export **traces**. Everything is OTLP. A single collector fans each signal out to one or more backends of your choice.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  R["Registry / Auth / MCP Gateway"] -->|"OTLP metrics"| C["OTel Collector<br/>(vendor-neutral seam)"]
  A["Agents (OpenLLMetry)"] -->|"OTLP traces + bearer token"| GW["OTel Gateway"] --> C
  C -->|"exporter(s)"| Ref["Grafana + Prometheus + Tempo<br/>(reference backend)"]
  C -->|"exporter(s)"| Vendor["New Relic · Datadog · Splunk · Grafana Cloud · …"]
```

- **Metrics path** — platform services emit performance and usage data that shows what your system is doing: request counts, latency, error rates, and resource utilization.
- **Traces path** — AI agents emit detailed execution traces that show what LLMs are doing: which models are called, how many tokens are used, and how long requests take.
- **Backends** — route your telemetry to any observability platform you already use, or multiple at once, without changing application code.

---

## Connecting an Observability Backend

All telemetry flows through the **OpenTelemetry Collector**, which is where you configure which backend receives your data. The collector receives OTLP from platform services and agents, then exports to one or more backends through **exporters**.

To connect a backend, add its exporter configuration and reference it in the pipeline:

```yaml
exporters:
  otlphttp/vendor:                 # most backends accept OTLP natively
    endpoint: https://otlp.<vendor>.example.com
    headers:
      api-key: ${env:VENDOR_API_KEY}

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      exporters: [otlp/tempo, otlphttp/vendor]          # fan out to both
    metrics:
      exporters: [prometheusremotewrite, otlphttp/vendor]
```

You can export to **multiple backends simultaneously** — useful for migrating vendors, dual-shipping for redundancy, or sending traces to one tool and metrics to another.

| Backend | How the collector ships to it |
|---|---|
| **Grafana / Prometheus / Tempo** | Prometheus + Tempo exporters (self-hosted reference) |
| **Grafana Cloud** | OTLP exporter to the Grafana Cloud OTLP endpoint |
| **New Relic** | OTLP exporter (OTLP-native endpoint + license-key header) |
| **Datadog** | `datadog` exporter, or Datadog's OTLP intake |
| **Splunk** | OTLP to Splunk Observability Cloud, or `splunk_hec` exporter |
| **Others (Honeycomb, Dynatrace, Elastic, …)** | OTLP exporter |

---

## Platform Metrics

The platform captures performance and operational metrics from all services:

- **Registry operations** — request counts and latency for list, search, create, update, and delete operations
- **MCP activity** — tool discovery, tool execution, server requests, resource access, and prompt execution with latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99)
- **Auth operations** — authentication requests, token validation, session management, and OAuth flow metrics

These metrics power dashboards that show registry operations, MCP gateway traffic, and authentication activity.

---

## Agent LLM Traces

AI agents emit detailed execution traces that capture:

- **Model and provider** — which LLM model and AI provider was used for each request
- **Token usage** — input and output tokens for cost tracking and usage analysis
- **Request latency** — execution time and performance metrics

The reference Grafana dashboard visualizes LLM call rates, latency percentiles (p95), and token usage broken down by agent, AI provider, and model. The same trace data is available in other observability platforms when configured through the collector.

![Agent LLM Observability dashboard — LLM call rate, p95 latency, and input/output token usage broken down by agent, AI provider, and model](../img/agent-llm-observability.png)

---

## Instrumentation Standard

The agent pipeline standardizes on **OpenLLMetry** as the single instrumentation layer across the fleet. Because it emits the **OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions** — a vendor-neutral attribute set — the captured data is portable across backends, and any agent appears automatically the moment it emits the standard `gen_ai.*` attributes.

Two environment settings keep the fleet consistent:

- **`OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=gen_ai_latest_experimental`** — selects the latest GenAI conventions so token usage lands under `gen_ai.usage.input_tokens` / `output_tokens`.
- **`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`** (or the OpenLLMetry equivalent) — points the agent at the gateway. Telemetry is a no-op when unset, so local and CI runs are unaffected.

---

## Privacy & Content Controls

By default, LLM instrumentation can record the full prompt and completion text as span attributes. The agent pipeline disables this so user payloads never reach any backend:

- **`TRACELOOP_TRACE_CONTENT=false`** — records only metadata (model, token counts, latency) and drops prompt/completion content (`gen_ai.input.messages`, `gen_ai.output.messages`, and prompt/completion attributes). Set it to `true` only in approved environments because doing so allows supported LLM instrumentations to include prompts and completions in exported telemetry spans.

Content is suppressed **at the source**, so it is never transmitted to the collector — and therefore never to any downstream vendor. Token counts and model metadata are unaffected, so usage and cost views keep working. The platform metrics path carries no content by design (counts and durations only).

---

## Securing the Telemetry Endpoint

Platform metrics travel service-to-collector inside the cluster and remain private. Agent traces flow through an external gateway, and how you expose that endpoint determines the security posture.

### Default: public endpoint with bearer auth

The gateway is exposed through a public load balancer with TLS termination and bearer-token authentication. This works from anywhere but the OTLP endpoint is reachable from the internet.

### More secure: private VPC endpoint

When agents run in the same virtual private network as the gateway (for example, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime with VPC connectivity, Azure Container Apps with VNET integration, or GCP Cloud Run with VPC connector), keep the endpoint entirely private:

- Use an **internal load balancer** with private IPs only, unreachable from the internet
- Agents send OTLP to the load balancer's private DNS name, which resolves within the VPC
- Bearer-token authentication provides defense-in-depth
- TLS termination is optional since traffic never leaves the private network

| Aspect | Public endpoint | Private VPC endpoint |
|---|---|---|
| Internet exposure | Reachable publicly | Private IPs only |
| Auth | Bearer token + TLS | Bearer token (TLS optional) |
| Network scope | Anywhere | Same VPC/VNET |

!!! note "Cross-account or cross-VPC scenarios"
    For cross-account or cross-VPC scenarios, use your cloud provider's private connectivity service (AWS PrivateLink, Azure Private Link, GCP Private Service Connect) to extend the internal endpoint without traversing the public internet.

---

## Next Steps

- [Security Control Design](../design/security-design.md) — How authentication, RBAC, and ACL compose across the platform
- [AgentCore Federation](agentcore-federation.md) — Connecting Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gateways to the registry
- [Registry Endpoint](registry-endpoint.md) — How clients discover and invoke resources through the gateway

**Product page & demo**

- Learn more about governed AI and product demos on ASCENDING: [Governed AI product page](https://ascendingdc.com/jarvis-ai/governed-ai/).

# Walkthroughs: Test MCP Access with Two Users

Published URL: https://jarvisregistry.com/walkthroughs/mcp-access-control/
Source Markdown: docs/walkthroughs/mcp-access-control.md

# Validate MCP access with two users and synthetic data

Before connecting a business system, check whether your Jarvis Registry deployment stops an unauthorized user from calling a registered MCP server, even when that user knows its server ID and tool name. This walkthrough uses two identities, one harmless tool, and a permission change.

The outcomes below are **acceptance criteria to validate on your deployment**, not a report of a completed tenant test. The included local probe checks the sample MCP server; it does not test Registry authentication or authorization.

Use the [MCP Gateway guide](../features/mcp-gateway-registry.md) for registration and sharing, and [Registry Endpoint](../features/registry-endpoint.md) for client connection setup. This walkthrough adds a repeatable access check to those workflows.

## Understand the access boundaries

**Roles define application capabilities; ACLs define access to specific resources.** To call a registered MCP server, the user's role must allow the action and the server's ACL must grant access. Both are required.

| Control | What it checks | Limit of this exercise |
|---|---|---|
| Application role | Allows gateway calls (`mcp-proxy-ops`) or server metadata reads (`servers-read`). | These capabilities do not grant access to a particular server. |
| Server access-control list (ACL) | Grants access to the particular server; `execute_tool` checks it on every invocation. | Knowing the server ID or discovering it earlier does not grant access. |
| Disabled tools | A server owner can disable tools for all consumers through normal discovery and `execute_tool`. | This is not a per-user permission, and the transparent proxy does not enforce this list. |
| Downstream authorization | The downstream service and the credentials used for the request determine access to business operations and records. | A synthetic server-access test cannot prove record-level permissions in a business system. |

The transparent proxy and the Registry gateway are different execution paths. The proxy checks server ACLs, but does not apply `disabledTools`. Repeat the server-access checks in the connection mode your clients use; do not infer one mode's tool restrictions from another. See the [tool-enablement contract](../design/mcp-tool-enablement-api.md).

## Before you start

Use an isolated, non-production Registry deployment and synthetic data only. If you need a deployment first, follow the [Deployment Guide](../deployment-guide.md).

- **Alice** has the built-in power-user role and owns the test server. Her role allows the setup actions; ownership grants her access to this server.
- **Bob** has the built-in user role, including the `mcp-proxy-ops` and `servers-read` scopes, but no ACL grant on the test server. Do not use the read-only role: it lacks the gateway capability.
- Use separate browser profiles and client sessions with separate credentials. Verify each authenticated identity before testing.
- Keep the test server private: turn off **Everyone** and avoid any group grant that includes Bob. Retain Alice as owner throughout.
- Use a client that lets you inspect discovery results and invoke explicit tools. Record the deployed Registry version, client version, connection mode, and test server ID.

Verify each session or token includes the required scopes; a down-scoped token can have fewer capabilities than its user's role. See [RBAC and scopes](../design/scopes.md). Entra deployments should also follow [Configure Entra scope groups](../runbooks/entra-scope-groups.md); a same-named group is not a substitute for the configured group Object ID.

## 1. Check the synthetic MCP server locally

The included [synthetic server](examples/mcp/synthetic_mcp_server.py) exposes one tool, `lookup_synthetic_ticket`. It returns a fabricated ticket and makes no external requests. It has no credentials, customer records, write tools, or authentication.

From the repository root, with the repository dependencies available, start it in one terminal:

```sh
uv run python docs/walkthroughs/examples/mcp/synthetic_mcp_server.py --port 8879
```

From the repository root in another terminal, run the [protocol probe](examples/mcp/probe_synthetic_mcp.py):

```sh
uv run python docs/walkthroughs/examples/mcp/probe_synthetic_mcp.py --port 8879
```

The probe connects to `http://127.0.0.1:8879/mcp`, initializes an MCP session, lists tools, and makes three calls. Its acceptance criteria are:

- `tools/list` contains `lookup_synthetic_ticket` with the required `ticket_id` input.
- Calling it with `{"ticket_id":"SYNTHETIC-1"}` succeeds and returns this structured content:

```json
{"ticket_id": "SYNTHETIC-1", "status": "open", "synthetic": true}
```

- Calling it with an unknown ticket ID or without the required argument returns a tool error.

Resolve any probe failure before diagnosing Registry permissions. A successful probe establishes only that the local sample works.

### Keep the network boundary intact

The sample binds only to `127.0.0.1` and has no authentication. **Never expose it publicly.** A Registry process can use the URL above only if it shares that host's network context. A container's loopback address refers to the container itself; a remote Registry cannot reach your laptop's loopback address. Adding `host.docker.internal` alone does not make a loopback-only listener reachable.

For the Registry portion, run the sample in the same isolated network context as Registry, or use an approved private synthetic endpoint reachable from Registry. Establish that arrangement before registering the URL. Do not change the sample to listen on a public interface to make the test work.

## 2. Register and enable a private test server

As Alice:

1. Follow the [MCP server registration workflow](../features/mcp-gateway-registry.md#registering-an-mcp-server). Use Streamable HTTP and the synthetic endpoint that Registry can actually reach. Select **No Auth** only for the isolated sample described above.
2. Keep **Everyone** off and confirm Bob has no direct or group grant. Verify Alice is the owner.
3. Enable the server and complete any required authorization. Enabling fetches its tools and schedules search indexing. If tools are missing, use the deployment's capabilities-refresh flow and inspect the resulting status before continuing.
4. Read the saved server details and tool catalog. Record the actual server ID, downstream tool name, and input schema. `GET /api/v1/servers/{server_id}/tools` reads the cached catalog; it does not itself fetch tools from the downstream server.
5. Wait until Alice can discover the tool through the Registry endpoint. If she cannot, resolve reachability, enablement, capabilities, or indexing first.

**Acceptance criteria:** Alice owns a private, enabled server; its saved catalog contains the synthetic tool; Registry discovery returns that tool for Alice. Registration success alone is insufficient.

## 3. Compare discovery and explicit execution

Connect Alice and Bob to the Registry endpoint in separate sessions. In each, call `discover_servers` with the same query, for example these tool arguments:

```json
{"query": "lookup synthetic ticket", "top_n": 20, "type_list": ["tool"]}
```

From Alice's matching result, copy the exact `server_id` and `tool_name` from the same entity. Inspect `input_schema`; if it is absent, use the saved tool catalog. Do not derive the downstream name from a display label or wrapper name.

Invoke the Registry tool named `execute_tool` in both sessions using the same arguments:

```json
{
  "server_id": "REPLACE_WITH_THE_ACTUAL_SERVER_ID",
  "tool_name": "lookup_synthetic_ticket",
  "arguments": {"ticket_id": "SYNTHETIC-1"}
}
```

Use the actual discovered tool name if testing another approved synthetic endpoint. Give Bob the known test identifiers even if his search returns nothing. This deliberately checks whether execution is denied independently of discovery.

**Acceptance criteria to validate:**

| Check | Alice, owner | Bob, no server grant |
|---|---|---|
| Discover the synthetic tool | The matching tool appears. | The test server's tool does not appear. |
| Call the known tool through `execute_tool` | The synthetic result returns after any required consent. | The result has `isError: true` and an access-denied message; the tool invocation is not forwarded downstream. |
| Read server tools or metadata | The saved details are accessible. | The details are denied. |

Complete any client consent or downstream authorization flow before counting an allowed call as successful, then retry. A consent prompt is not a completed tool call. An empty discovery result alone does not prove an ACL denial: indexing or an ACL-service failure can also prevent results.

Inspect the response body as well as HTTP status. MCP tool errors can arrive in an HTTP 200 response. Use the deployment's available request logs or traces to correlate denied and allowed calls with downstream activity; a UI message alone does not demonstrate that no tool invocation was forwarded.

If clients connect directly through the transparent MCP proxy, repeat the allowed and denied tool calls through each user's configured proxy connection. Use the connection URL supplied by the deployment. Validate server-ACL denial separately from the `execute_tool` result, and record the actual proxy response.

## 4. Grant Bob access, then remove it

1. As Alice, open the server's sharing panel and grant Bob **VIEW**. Save and read back the permissions.
2. In Bob's existing client session, repeat the same `execute_tool` call. Complete any required consent and retry.
3. Remove Bob's direct grant and save. Verify that no group grant or **Everyone** setting still grants him access.
4. Repeat the call in Bob's existing session, then after a fresh sign-in. Record both results and timestamps. If transparent proxy connections are in scope, repeat those calls too.
5. Repeat Alice's call to check that her owner access still works.

**Acceptance criteria:** Bob's call succeeds after the grant and is denied after all applicable grants are removed, without forwarding the denied tool invocation. Alice continues to succeed. Validate and record the actual behavior and timing for both existing and fresh sessions.

`execute_tool` checks the server ACL on every invocation. This does not promise immediate global token or session revocation. The resolver considers direct, group, and public grants using Registry's stored membership information; removing an IdP group membership is a separate operation from removing a server ACL. The [Entra runbook](../runbooks/entra-scope-groups.md) also states that existing tokens are not automatically revoked by configuration changes. An access change cannot recall an already completed call or previously returned data.

## 5. Test server-wide tool disabling separately

Grant Bob VIEW again so both users can access the server. Confirm both can call the harmless tool before testing its disabled state.

As Alice, use the server's tool controls to disable `lookup_synthetic_ticket`. The equivalent API is:

```text
PATCH /api/v1/servers/{server_id}/tools
```

For a dedicated test server whose disabled list was initially empty, the request body is:

```json
{"disabledTools": ["lookup_synthetic_ticket"]}
```

This replaces the **entire** disabled list. Read and retain the previous list first, preserve its entries when adding the test tool, and read back the saved response. Names are checked against the cached tool catalog; unknown names are silently dropped. Updating the list requires `servers-write` scope and the server's owner-only `SHARE` permission.

**Acceptance criteria to validate:**

- `execute_tool` rejects the disabled tool for both users with `isError: true`, before forwarding a tool invocation.
- Normal `discover_servers` results omit it once the search index reflects the change. Index updates are best-effort, so a result may briefly remain visible; execution reads the server document and should still reject it.
- After restoring the original disabled list, both users can call the tool again while their server grants remain in place.

The transparent proxy does **not** enforce `disabledTools`. Do not treat hiding or disabling a tool through the Registry gateway as a capability boundary for every client mode. A requirement such as “Alice can call tool A but Bob cannot, while both access this server” needs a separate authorization design; this server-wide switch does not provide it. See [MCP Tool Enablement API](../design/mcp-tool-enablement-api.md).

## 6. Record results and restore the test setup

For each acceptance check, retain the user alias, deployed version, client and connection mode, server ID, tool name, timestamp, sanitized result, and whether the downstream tool invocation was observed. Include a request or trace ID when available. Observability availability depends on deployment configuration; see [Observability](../features/observability.md).

| Observation | What to check next |
|---|---|
| Bob still succeeds after his direct grant is removed | Confirm the authenticated identity, remaining group/public grants, stored group membership, and deployed version. |
| Search hides the tool but execution succeeds | Identify the connection mode and read back the saved disabled-tool names. |
| `execute_tool` returns “Service temporarily unavailable” | Investigate ACL lookup availability; this is an operational failure, not proof of a policy denial. |
| An allowed call produces consent or authentication prompts | Complete the approved authorization flow and repeat before assessing the result. |
| HTTP status is successful but the tool result is an error | Inspect `isError`, content, and any JSON-RPC error. |

Use synthetic inputs throughout: the gateway implementation logs the MCP request body, including tool arguments. Remove tokens, cookies, personal identifiers, and sensitive payloads from any retained evidence.

Restore the original sharing and disabled-tool settings, disconnect the test clients, and stop the local sample with Ctrl+C when finished. Keep only the sanitized acceptance record. Passing these checks establishes behavior for the tested version, identities, and connection modes; it does not establish downstream record-level authorization or a compliance certification.

## Implementation references

- [Gateway execution and per-call ACL checks](https://github.com/ascending-llc/jarvis-registry/blob/01372e3c80baa1b8833d6851acabb41497b89d2d/registry/src/registry/mcpgw/tools/server.py#L368-L470)
- [Server ACL resolution](https://github.com/ascending-llc/jarvis-registry/blob/01372e3c80baa1b8833d6851acabb41497b89d2d/registry/src/registry/services/access_control_service.py#L577-L632) and [shared user/group/public principal resolution](https://github.com/ascending-llc/jarvis-registry/blob/01372e3c80baa1b8833d6851acabb41497b89d2d/registry-pkgs/src/registry_pkgs/access_control.py)
- [Discovery ACL and enabled-tool filters](https://github.com/ascending-llc/jarvis-registry/blob/01372e3c80baa1b8833d6851acabb41497b89d2d/registry/src/registry/services/search/service.py#L132-L211)
- [Transparent proxy access checks](https://github.com/ascending-llc/jarvis-registry/blob/01372e3c80baa1b8833d6851acabb41497b89d2d/registry/src/registry/api/proxy_routes.py#L1024-L1035)
- [Scope definitions and built-in group mappings](https://github.com/ascending-llc/jarvis-registry/blob/01372e3c80baa1b8833d6851acabb41497b89d2d/registry-pkgs/src/registry_pkgs/scopes.yml)
- [Server enablement, capabilities, and disabled-tool updates](https://github.com/ascending-llc/jarvis-registry/blob/01372e3c80baa1b8833d6851acabb41497b89d2d/registry/src/registry/services/server_service.py#L835-L985)
